cases.abstract: ConvNeXt investigates whether a convolutional architecture can match hierarchical vision Transformers by adopting their training and design choices without attention. Starting from a ResNet baseline with modernized training, we hold the recipe fixed while progressively changing the architecture at approximately controlled computational cost. The block separates spatial from channel mixing: a large depthwise kernel operates before channel expansion, limiting spatial-processing cost while pointwise layers provide capacity. Evaluation covers ImageNet classification, COCO detection and instance segmentation, and ADE20K semantic segmentation. At 384 x 384 resolution, ImageNet-1K-trained ConvNeXt-B achieves 85.1% top-1 accuracy versus Swin-B's 84.5%, with V100 inference throughput of 95.7 versus 85.1 images per second. Scaling both model size and pretraining data yields 87.8% for ConvNeXt-XL after ImageNet-22K pretraining and ImageNet-1K fine-tuning at that resolution. ConvNeXt is also competitive with similarly sized Swin backbones on downstream tasks. These comparisons identify a convolutional route to competitive recognition at both training scales, without Swin's specialized attention modules.
cases.methods: Large spatial kernels broaden coverage but become more expensive at greater channel widths. ConvNeXt places its 7 x 7 depthwise convolution before channel expansion, so spatial mixing uses the narrower input width. Two pointwise convolutions then expand channels fourfold and restore them, assigning channel mixing to dense operations. Each residual block retains one GELU and one layer normalization. Separate stride-two convolutions perform stage transitions, with additional normalization at changes in resolution; introducing these transitions without that normalization caused training to diverge. The architecture is developed through sequential ResNet modifications under a fixed 300-epoch recipe using AdamW, augmentation, and regularization, with FLOPs roughly controlled. Small-model accuracies average three training seeds. This sequence measures how successive combined designs behave under common training conditions: it supports the final convolutional construction, but does not independently isolate every component's effect.
cases.results: The classification comparison with Swin-B shows that higher accuracy need not require lower inference throughput in the tested setting. With ImageNet-1K training and 384 x 384 inputs, ConvNeXt-B reaches 85.1% versus 84.5% top-1 accuracy, 95.7 versus 85.1 images per second on V100, and 45.0 versus 47.1 GFLOPs. That is a favorable comparison with a similarly sized Transformer, not the highest accuracy in the training group: EfficientNetV2-L reaches 85.7% with 480 x 480 inputs and 53.0 GFLOPs. After ImageNet-22K pretraining, Cascade Mask R-CNN with ConvNeXt-B obtains 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP, versus Swin-B's 53.0 and 45.8. Under the same pretraining regime, UperNet with 640 x 640 crops and multi-scale testing reaches 53.1 versus 51.7 mIoU on ADE20K. The downstream comparisons extend the case for competitive convolutional features to dense prediction; they measure prediction quality rather than the classification speed benefit.
cases.notes: Abstract and Methods preserve the block's cost rationale: spatial mixing precedes channel expansion (Sections 2.3-2.5). Results distinguish the accuracy-throughput comparison from dense prediction accuracy (Tables 1, 3, 4), retaining EfficientNetV2-L's higher ImageNet-1K accuracy. The modernization sequence ends at 82.0%, while Table 1 lists 82.1% for ConvNeXt-T; no reconciliation is assumed. Sequential changes do not isolate all component effects. Throughput values are V100 classification measurements, not COCO FPS on A100.

cases.abstract: Fast radiance-field fitting does not ensure that a reconstructed scene can be explored interactively. We represent static scenes with anisotropic 3D Gaussians that project directly into image-space splats, allowing the same primitives to support optimization and fast rasterization. For photographic scenes, sparse structure-from-motion points initialize geometry; joint updates of geometry and directional color are interleaved with cloning, splitting, and pruning to allocate detail. A differentiable tile renderer shares depth sorting across pixels for approximate blending and reuses those lists for backpropagation without a fixed limit on splats receiving gradients. Evaluation covers 13 real scenes and synthetic bounded scenes. At 30,000 iterations, real-dataset averages reach 134-154 frames per second at native image resolutions on an A6000 after approximately 27-42 minutes of optimization. Quality is competitive with Mip-NeRF360 but metric-dependent: on its dataset, SSIM and LPIPS improve while PSNR remains lower. The speed-quality benefit is accompanied by substantially larger stored models than neural radiance fields, artifacts in poorly observed regions, and occasional popping.
cases.methods: Gradient computation must accommodate varying numbers of blended splats without storing a separate variable-length list for every pixel. Projected Gaussians are assigned to overlapping 16 x 16 pixel tiles, each instance receiving a key combining tile identity with view-space depth. One GPU radix sort creates reusable ordered lists for all tiles. The forward pass blends color and opacity front to back until opacity saturates, rather than truncating after a fixed splat count. The backward pass traverses the same lists in reverse, reconstructing intermediate opacity values from the stored final accumulation. This replaces per-pixel contribution histories with shared tile lists while allowing all blended contributors to receive gradients. Rendering losses update Gaussian geometry, opacity, and spherical harmonic color, interleaved with gradient-guided cloning and splitting. Because depth order is shared within tiles rather than recomputed for each pixel, visibility-aware blending is approximate.
cases.results: Gaussian splatting's rendering speed coexists with mixed quality relative to Mip-NeRF360. On the latter's dataset, the 30,000-iteration model achieves SSIM of 0.815 versus 0.792 and LPIPS of 0.214 versus 0.237, but lower PSNR, 27.21 versus 27.69 dB. The model renders at 134 frames per second on an A6000 after an average 41 minutes 33 seconds of fitting, but stores 734 MB of parameters versus Mip-NeRF360's 8.6 MB. Within the Gaussian method, longer fitting trades speed for quality: on Tanks & Temples, moving from 7,000 to 30,000 iterations raises PSNR from 21.20 to 23.14 dB while reducing rendering from 197 to 154 frames per second. A separate Truck ablation at 30,000 iterations tests the renderer's gradient design: limiting gradients to ten splats lowers PSNR from 24.81 to 13.84 dB. This supports retaining gradients for all blended contributors in that setting. Artifacts persist in poorly observed regions, and occasional popping remains.
cases.notes: Abstract and Methods connect reusable tile lists to rendering and gradient computation (Section 6); Results test that gradient choice using the separate Truck ablation (Table 3). Main-table Mip-NeRF360 quality scores on its own dataset come from its publication. Its reported 48-hour training figure aggregates four A100 GPUs running for 12 hours, not A6000 wall time; no matched-hardware speedup is claimed. Ablation inputs were separately downsampled. Storage comparisons concern optimized parameters, not peak training memory, which can exceed 20 GB. SfM initialization is scoped to photographic scenes; the bounded synthetic evaluation uses random initialization.
